questions.label: Part 1 (e)
questions.q: What is the difference between functions and relations on sets? Can a function be defined as a relation? What about vice-versa?
questions.a:
A relation between two sets A and B is a subset of A × B. A function φ : A ↦ B is a relation on A and B such that for every x ∈ A there exists at most one y ∈ B such that (x, y) ∈ φ. When such a y exists, it is denoted by φ(x). By definition a function is a relation.

A relation R between two sets A and B can be viewed as a function fR from A to 2B, that is, fR : A ↦ 2B: for each element a ∈ A, fR(a) denotes the set of elements in B (possibly none) that are in R-relation with a. For example, consider the less-than < and greater-than > relations between natural numbers. Then, f<(3) = {0, 1, 2} and f>(3) = {4, 5, 6, . . .} = {n | n > 3}.

questions.label: Part 2 (b)
questions.q: Prove, by contradiction, that for all integers n, if n2 is odd, then n is odd.
questions.a:
Suppose that n is an integer such that n2 is odd, but n is even. Hence, n = 2 × k, for some integer k. So, by substitution we have

n2 = (2 × k) × (2 × k) = 2(2 × k × k)

Now, (2×k×k) is an integer because products of integers are integer; and 2 and k are integers. Hence, n2 = 2×k′, where k′ = (2 × k × k) is an integer. It follows then that n2 is even. This contradicts the supposition that n2 is odd. Hence, integer n ought to be odd.

questions.label: Part 2 (c)
questions.q: Let A and B be two finite sets such that |A| = |B| and let φ : A ↦ B be a total function. Show that φ is surjective if and only if φ is injective.
questions.a: Since φ is total, domain of φ is A. If φ is injective as well, then the range of φ is B. Therefore, |A| = |φ(A)| = |B|. Hence, φ is surjective. Conversely, if φ is surjective, then for all y ∈ B there exists a x ∈ A such that φ(x) = y. Since φ is total, it also holds that for all x ∈ A there exists a y ∈ B such that φ(x) = y. Hence, φ is injective.

questions.label: Part 4 (b)
questions.q:
Consider the following recursively defined function weird(m, n)

weird(m, n) = if m = 0 then n + 1

if n = 0 then weird(m − 1, 1)

weird(m − 1, weird(m, n − 1)) otherwise

For example weird(0, 0) = 1 and weird(1, 0) = weird(0, 1) = 2.

What can you evaluate about this function?

Hint: First consider weird(0, 1), weird(0, 2), weird(0, 3), ... and then weird(1, 1), weird(1, 2), weird(1, 3), ... and then weird(2, 1), weird(2, 2), weird(2, 3), ... etc. You can write a program to help you if you wish.
questions.a:
This is known as Ackermann’s function, and it is famous for a very high rate of growth.

It is not hard to see that weird(0, n) = n + 1, weird(1, n) = n + 2 and weird(2, n) = 2n + 3. But weird(3, n) = 2n+3 − 3 and weird(4, n) = 22..2 − 3, where there are n + 3 powers of 2 (!!). This is sometimes written as 2 ↑↑ (n + 3) − 3. weird(4, 2) is a number with 19,729 digits (!!!). For this reason this function is often described as a generalised exponential.

questions.a:
1. For languages requiring strict ordering e.g., (ab)∗ or three consecutive 1s the easier way is to construct a DFA as there may be only one way to generate the strings. See that, trivially, every DFA is also a NFA.

3. NFAs are generally smaller in size as compared to DFAs. Because of this, it may be practical to construct NFAs as opposed to DFAs.

questions.label: Part 2 (c)
questions.q: Using the “Tools” menu, convert it to a DFA. Do you notice any differences from this DFA to the one showed in this sheet? Are these DFAs equivalent? Can you explain why Automatarium had to create the states shown?
questions.a:
The conversion algorithm creates a state for every possible combination of NFA states a string can reach:

• The DFA q5 simulates that after reading a “ba”, we can either be in the NFA states q2 or q4.

• If we read an “a” or “c”, then we have two possibilites:

– The NFA moved to q4 after reading a “ba”. In this case, the NFA will stay in q4.

– The NFA stayed in q2 after reading a “ba” (due to the non-deterministic self-loop in q2). In this case, the NFA will stay in q2.

Therefore for any “a”’s or “c”’s after a “ba” we can only be in the NFA states q2 or q4. This translates to state q5 in the DFA.

• If there is a “b” after our detected “ba”, then we need to account for three possibilities:

– The NFA moved to q4 after reading a “ba”. In this case, the NFA will stay in q4 for any “b”’s as well. – The NFA stayed in q2 after reading a “ba” and stayed in q2 after reading a “b”.

– The NFA stayed in q2 after reading a “ba” but moved to q3 after reading a “b”

Therefore, when reading a “b” after a “ba”, the NFA can be in states q2, q3 or q4. In the conversion to a DFA, this means we need to create a new state for this combination: q6 in Automatarium.

• Since both DFA states q5 and q6 correspond to subsets of NFA states with at least one final state (q4 in the NFA), both become final in the DFA as well.

The fact the resulting DFA contains redundant states is not a problem in theory. If you’re interested in how to minimise the number of states in a DFA, read the optional (non-examinable) Section 2.4 in the Linz book.

questions.label: Part 2 (c)
questions.q:
Which of the following languages can be represented by regular expressions? (A ‘yes’ or ‘no’ answer will suffice, you do not need to give the regular expression)

i. The set of all words contained in {0, 1}∗ that have an even number of 0’s and an odd number of 1’s.

ii. The set of all words contained in {0, 1}∗ whose lengths are divisible (i.e., with no remainder) by 3.

iii. The set of all words contained in {0, 1}∗ that do not contain ‘101‘ as a substring.

iv. The set of all words with the same number of 0’s and 1’s.
questions.a:
All but the last one. The question only asks you to give a true/false answer. For the most part, these regular expressions are very ugly and cumbersome, and we don’t expect you to give them; this question is more testing your knowledge about the expressive power of the different ways of representing languages.

Some students have trouble accepting the fact that some of these languages can be represented as regular expressions, because they are unable to find the regular expressions yourselves. So here is an example for the first one, to give you a sense of how ugly representing languages as regular expressions can be compared to other representations.

We can represent the given language as a DFA like this:

Here the label qee means that, in this state, we have an even number of 0’s and an even number of 1’s; qoe means that, in this state, we have an odd number of 0’s and an even number of 1’s, and so on. The final state is qeo, where we have an even number of 0’s and an odd number of 1’s (as acceptance into the language requires) and is denoted by a double circle. The initial state (even 0’s, even 1’s) is denoted by an arrow. Starting at the initial state, we can trace any string we like following the transitions, and if at the end of the string trace we end up in state qeo, that means the word is accepted as a member of the language; if not, then it is rejected.

But what has all of this got to do with regular expressions, though? I hear you ask..

Regular expressions and finite state automata have the same expressive power; that is, anything that can be represented as a finite state automata can be represented as a regular expression, and vice-versa. There are a number of algorithms that can be used to convert between FSA’s and regular expressions (some of them are detailed [here]), but you can also just build the FSA in JFLAP and then use the convert tool to give you the regular expression. This is the result you get from converting it using JFLAP:

((0(11)∗0)∗(1 + 0(11)∗10)(00 + 01(11)∗10)∗(1 + 01(11)∗0))∗(0(11)∗0)∗(1 + 0(11)∗10)(00 + 01(11)∗10)∗

Pretty ugly, huh? So while you may have trouble building the actual regular expressions themselves, this question is asking you to think about the expressive power of regular expressions. Even though the expression may be really long and cumbersome, if there is no need to keep track of exactly how many of each character is in each string, then it can be expressed as a regular expression or FSA. When you need to keep track of how many of each character, then you may need something with greater expressive power.

Thanks to tutor Angus Kenny for developing this full answer!

Let G be the grammar

iv. If you find the above grammar to be ambiguous, construct an unambiguous grammar equivalent to G; otherwise justify why it is unambiguous.
questions.a:
It is ambiguous precisely because of the reason stated in the previous question. If you can work out a way to force an order of generating as and bs (e.g. as first, bs second), you can remove the ambiguity.

S → AB | SS

A → aA | a

B → bB | b

In this, because we are either doing a left-most or right-most derivation, we must expand either the A or B rule first. From either of these rules, there is no way to get back up to the S rule, so we cannot decide to expand bs after deciding to expand as.

Another answer could be:

S → SA | A

A → aA | aB

B → bB | b

This version will always expand as before bs regardless of a left-most or right-most derivation (which doesn’t make it better, it’s just a different way of seeing it).

The centre marker c tells the machine exactly where the middle is, so no guessing is needed:

δ(q0, a, X) = {(q0, aX)}, δ(q0, b, X) = {(q0, bX)} for every X ∈{a, b, z},

δ(q0, c, X) = {(q1, X)} for every X ∈{a, b, z}, δ(q1, a, a) = {(q1, λ)}, δ(q1, b, b) = {(q1, λ)},

δ(q1, λ, z) = {(q2, z)}, F = {q2}.

questions.a:
Use the stack as a signed counter: push a 0 for an unmatched a, a 1 for an unmatched b, and cancel opposite symbols.

δ(q0, a, z) = {(q0, 0z)}, δ(q0, b, z) = {(q0, 1z)}, δ(q0, a, 0) = {(q0, 00)}, δ(q0, b, 1) = {(q0, 11)},

δ(q0, b, 0) = {(q0, λ)}, δ(q0, a, 1) = {(q0, λ)}, δ(q0, λ, z) = {(q1, z)}, F = {q1}.

The stack holds only the surplus of whichever symbol currently leads; it returns to z exactly when the counts are equal.

questions.q: Using the npda from the example, give the instantaneous descriptions accepting aabb, and give the leftmost derivation of aabb in G. What is the correspondence between the two?

questions.label: Part 5 (d)
questions.q: Reflection. Where do pushdown automata sit in the language hierarchy? Sketch the relationship between regular languages, deterministic context-free languages, and context-free languages, and name the machine associated with each. How does this relate to context-free grammars?
questions.a: regular ⊊ DCFL ⊊ context-free, each inclusion strict. The associated machines are: finite automaton (regular), deterministic PDA (DCFL), nondeterministic PDA (context-free). Nondeterministic PDAs accept exactly the context-free languages, the same class generated by context-free grammars, so grammars and npdas are two descriptions of one class. Unlike finite automata, deterministic and nondeterministic PDAs are not equivalent.

Branch C (allow any a’s, then enforce j = k):

questions.label: Part 6 (c)
questions.q: (Determinism reasoning.) Let L = {anbncm | n, m ≥ 0} ∪{anbmcm | n, m ≥ 0}. Is L a deterministic context-free language? Justify.
questions.a: L is context-free but not deterministic. It is context-free because each half is, and an npda can guess at the start whether to match the a’s against the b’s (first set) or the b’s against the c’s (second set). It is not deterministic because, while reading the a’s and b’s, the machine cannot yet tell which equality it must eventually check (na = nb or nb = nc); that depends on symbols not yet read, so the choice cannot be made deterministically. Hence L is context-free but not a DCFL.

The only change is that the switch q0 → q1 is now caused by reading c rather than by a λ-move; because the marker removes the guess, the resulting machine is even deterministic.

questions.q: Build a Turing machine that enumerates the set of even length strings over {a}∗ (i.e., L((aa)∗) by writing them one after the other on the tape, each separated by #. Notice this machine should never terminate. You can define the full state diagram, but try to use the TM you created in the previous question and give a high level description instead.
questions.a:
Let’s call this TM M. We already defined a TM that writes w#w, let’s call it M1. Let’s define a few other “auxiliary” TMs:

• M2: moves the tape head to the right end of the tape, pointing to the first □ symbol at that end.

• M3: starting from the right end of the tape as above, writes a and move right.

• M4: starting from the right end of the tape as above, moves the tape head to the left one by one, until it finds a # symbol. Then move the tape head to the right, pointing to the first symbol after this #.

Convince yourself all these TMs exist (draw their state diagrams if required, they are quite simple).

With this, we can define M as:

1. Start from the empty string λ.

2. Run M1. This will copy the “last” string.

3. Run M2. This will ensure we are at the right end.

4. Run M3 twice. This adds aa to the copy we just made.

5. Run M4. This will leave us at the beginning of the last copied string (the one we appended aa to).

6. Go back to step 2. This will repeat the process, now copying the new string.

questions.label: Part 3 (a)
questions.q: Determine whether a Turing machine M halts on all inputs.
questions.a:
Suppose there does exist a machine X which is able to decide whether M halts on all inputs.

Let us build a Turing machine H, that takes a machine M and an input w, as follows:

• First, machine H takes M and builds from it an alternative Turing machine M w as follows: M w deletes the tape and writes w on it, and then operates like M (on the string w that was just written).

• Second, machine H runs X on M w.

We next show that H solve the Halting Problem::

• Suppose that M halts on input w. Then, M w will halt on any input, because it effectively is just deleting it and then running M on w, which halts. Hence, X will accept on input M w, and so will H on M and w.

• Suppose that M loops on input w. Then M w will loop on any input, as it effectively runs M on w anyways. So, X will reject and so will H, as expected.

This means that H solves the Halting Problem, a contradiction. Hence, X cannot exist and the problem is undecidable.

questions.label: Part 3 (c)
questions.q: Determine whether or not a Turing machine M when run on input w will ever reach a state q of M.
questions.a:
Suppose there does exist a machine X which is able to solve such problem. That is X receives M, w and q and decides whether M will ever reach state q when run on input w.

Let us build a Turing machine H as follows:

• First, machine H takes M and builds from it an alternative Turing machine Y as follows: Y operates exactly like M, but whenever a transition is not defined in M (and hence, M would halt), the machine Y transitions to a new state q not mentioned in M (that is Y has q but M has no state named q) and halts (no transition is defined for state q).

• After that, machine H runs X on Y , w, and q, and returns X’s output.

We next show that our TM H that we just build (using X) solves the Halting Problem:

• Suppose that M halts on input w. Then Y , when ran on w, will first execute like M and then transition to state q; so Y reaches q when ran on input w. So, X will accept when ran on input M, w and q, and so H will accept to (signaling that M halts as expected).

• Suppose that M loops on input w. This means that Y will also loop on w and will never reach its state q (as Y can only reach q when M halts). Then X will reject when ran on Y , w, and q, and so will H, as wanted. This means that H solves the Halting Problem, a contradiction. Hence, X cannot exist and the problem is undecidable.

We reduce the Halting problem to this problem to show that it is undecidable. Suppose there does exist a Turing machine X that is able to decide if two arbitrary Turing machines M1 and M2 halt on exactly the same inputs.

Let us build a Turing machine H as follows:

• First machine H takes M and w and builds a machine M w which simulates M being run on w.

• Then H creates a second, dummy machine M ′ which halts immediately.

• Finally, H runs X on M w and M ′ and accepts if X accepts.

We next show that H solves the Halting Problem:

• Suppose that M halts on input w. Then M w will always halt, as does M ′, so X will accept; which means that H accepts also.

• Suppose that M loops on input w. Then, M w will always loop, but M ′ halts, so X will reject; which means that H rejects also.

This means that H solves the Halting Problem, a contradiction. Hence, X cannot exist and the problem is undecidable.

questions.label: Part 3 (e)
questions.q: Determine whether a Turing machine M is such that L(M) is a regular language. Without loss of generality, assume the alphabet for L(M) is Σ = {a, b}. For this exercise, reduce from the TM Acceptance problem AT M instead.
questions.a:
We are to reduce AT M to our problem. Suppose we do have a Turing machine X that solves the regular problem. Let us build a Turing machine H as follows:

• First of all, H builds a special Turing machine W which has one input x as follows:

– If x is of the form anbn, then W accepts. This means that L(anbn) ⊆ L(W).

– If, on the other hand, x is not of the form anbn, then W simulates M on w, so it will accept x iff M accepts w (otherwise will reject or run forever, as M does).

• Second, H passes W to machine X

We can then show that H solves AT M, when given M on w:

• Suppose that M accepts w, that is, w ∈ L(M). Then L(W) = Σ∗ (i.e., W accepts all the strings). Why? if W is ran on a word of the shape anbn, W will accept it; and if run on a word not of that shape, then W will run M on w which will accept too: so every word will be accepted by W when M accepts w. So, when W is given to X, X will accept and so will H on M and w.

• Suppose that M does not accept w (may reject or run forever on w), that is, w∉ L(M). Then, W will only accept inputs of the form anbn (for any other input, M on w will be simulated, which does not accept). So, L(W) = L(anbn) which is not regular, and hence X will reject, and so will H, as expected,

This means that H solves the AT M, which is not possible as per question before. Hence, X cannot exist and the problem is undecidable.

questions.label: Part 4 (a)
questions.q: Prove that AT M is undecidable. Remember this is the TM Acceptance problem which is stated as “Determine whether a Turing machine M accepts an input w”.
questions.a:
We reduce the Halting problem to this problem to show that it is undecidable. Suppose there does exist a Turing machine X that is able to decide if a given Turing machine accepts an given input.

Let us build a Turing machine H as follows:

• First, machine H takes M and builds a machine M ′ that is exactly like M except that it makes all the states final states. So M ′ either accepts or runs forever.

• Then H runs X on M ′ and accepts if X accepts.

We next show that H solves the Halting Problem:

• Suppose that M halts on input w. Then M ′ will accept w. So, X will accept when run on M ′ and w (as all states in M ′ are now final), which means that H accepts too when run on M and w, as expected.

• Suppose that M does not halt on input w (i.e., it will run forever). Then, M ′ will run forever on w as well; and therefore X will reject when given M ′ and w. Thus H itself will reject on M and w, as expected.

This means that H solves the Halting Problem, a contradiction. Hence, X cannot exist and the problem is undecidable.

questions.label: Part 4 (b)
questions.q: Prove that EQT M is undecidable. Remember this is the TM Equivalence problem which is stated as “Determine whether two Turing machines M1 and M2 are such that L(M1) = L(M2)”.
questions.a:
We reduce the Halting problem to this problem to show that it is undecidable. Suppose there does exist a Turing machine X that is able to decide if L(M1) = L(M2), i.e., the languages of two arbitrary Turing machines M1 and M2 are the same.

Let us build a Turing machine H as follows:

• First machine H takes M and w and builds a machine M w which simulates M being run on w and accepts if M halts. This can be done by making all states that are “part of the simulated M” inside M w final states. • Then H creates a second, dummy machine M ′ which accepts everything.

• Finally, H runs X on M w and M ′ and accepts if X accepts.

We next show that H solves the Halting Problem:

• Suppose that M halts on input w. Then M w always accepts, as does M ′, so their languages are equivalent and X will accept; which means that H accepts also.

• Suppose that M does not halt on input w. Then, M w always loops, but M ′ always accepts, so their languages are not equivalent and X will reject; which means that H rejects also.

This means that H solves the Halting Problem, a contradiction. Hence, X cannot exist and the problem is undecidable.

questions.q:
Recall the Euclid algorithm to calculate the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) between two numbers. The GCD has the following property:

GCD(a, b) = GCD(b, a mod b)

Based on this, the Euclid algorithm can be defined as following (in an iterative way):

function gcd(a, b)
    while b != 0:
        t := b
        b := a mod b
        a := t
    return a

Implement the Euclid algorithm in OCaml using a recursive function.
questions.a: let rec gcd a b = if b = 0 then a else (gcd b (a mod b)) ;;

questions.label: Part 1 (d)
questions.q:
(Advanced, Optional) Let’s define a function to detect if a number is prime. Remember that a number d divides n if n mod d = 0. To detect if a number is prime, here is simple algorithm

function isprime(n)
    d := 2
    while d * d < n:
        if n mod d == 0:
            return false
    return true

In other words, starting from d = 2, we test if d can divide n and increment it until either we find a value that divides n or if the square of d is greater than n. Implement this algorithm in OCaml. Hint: you will need to define a recursive function, but that function will likely be an auxiliary function in your solution instead of the main function. Try coming up with a recursive solution in pseudocode first.
questions.a:
To get a recursive solution, we first need to notice that we want to return a boolean value. If we start from d = 2, two things can happen:

• If 2 ∗ 2 > n, we return true.

• Else, we then check if 2 divides n, if it does, return false. Else we proceed for d = d + 1 = 3.

The key thing is to realise that the second point above can be thought recursively. Here is a more general recipe: • If d ∗ d > n, we return true.

• Else:

– If nmodd = 0 we return false.

– Else we return whatever comes testing when from d := d + 1.

With this idea, we can define an auxiliary function:

let rec rec_divides d n =
    if d * d > n then false else
        if n mod d = 0 then true else rec_divides (d + 1) n

And now, we simply call this function using 2 as the first argument:

let isprime n = not (rec_divides 2 n)

questions.q: (Optional) Exponentation in https://lambdacalc.io/ (called power) is likely not defined in the same you did in the exercise above, even if your answer is correct. Can you explain the reasoning behind this alternative definition? (Warning: the interpretation is not trivial)
questions.a:
The alternative definition is:

exp := λn.λm.m n

Let’s take an example, like exp2 3 = 23. Here are the initial reduction steps:

exp 2 3 →β

(λn.λm.m n) 2 3 →β

(λm.m 2) 3 →β

3 2

Following the concept of Church numerals, this is equivalent to “apply the function 2 three tiimes”. Let’s check what happens when we do it:

3 2 →β

(λf.λx.f (f (f x))) 2 →β

λx.2 (2 (2 x)) →β

λx.(λf.λx.f (f x)) (2 (2 x))) →β

λx.λx.f (f x)[(2 (2 x))/f] →β

For the next step, notice that f ∈ FV (f (f x)) and x ∈ FV (2 (2 x))). This triggers a renaming before the substitution. Let’s rename x to x1

λx.λx.f (f x)[(2 (2 x))/f] →β

λx.λx1.f (f x)[x1/x][(2 (2 x))/f] →β

λx.λx1.f (f x1)[(2 (2 x))/f] →β

λx.λx1.(2 (2 x)) ((2 (2 x)) x1) →β

λx.λx1.2 (2 x) (2 (2 x) x1) →β

We removed parenthesis in the last step due to left-associativity. Notice how this new term calls the function 2 with two arguments: (2 x) and (2 (2 x) x1).

Let’s do one more reduction, but skipping a few steps and go straight into the definition of 2:

λx.λx1.2 (2 x) (2 (2 x) x1) →β

λx.λx1.(2 x) ((2 x) (2 (2 x) x1)) →β

λx.λx1.2 x (2 x (2 (2 x) x1)) →β

At this stage, notice how we are starting to get “sequences” of 2 x. Notice how this new term starts with λx.λx1. Ultimately, the normal form of this term will be a Church numeral that starts with λx.λx1 as opposed to λf.λx. But that doesn’t matter, as it is just renaming variables. What matters is that due to renaming, x should be “interpreted as f” and 2 x should be interpreted as “apply function x twice”.

With this, we can now see the reductions as “expanding the function x as a tree”. We will not finish the reduction here, but you can use the online calculator to see all the steps. But what the term 3 2 essentially does is creating a tree of height 3 where each node has 2 children. This will result in a total of 23 = 8 leaves, where each leaf calls the function x. Then, the resulting term is obtained by reading the leaves on a depth-first manner and composing each function each times it reaches a leaf. The end result should have “8 x’s” with x1 as the argument, which is the Church numeral for 8.

questions.label: Part 2 (d)
questions.q: Implement the equality operation between booleans: p = q. Then use this operation to define an alternative term for ⊕. You can use if for this exercise.
questions.a:
The equality predicate should return true when p = q and false otherwise. We can use a nested if approach for this:

eq := λp.λq.if p (if q true false) (if q false true)

This term is quite lenghty though. We can simplify this by noticing the internal if’s return either the predicate itself or its negation:

eq := λp.λq.if p q (¬ q)

Try a few reduction examples using values for p and q to convince yourself.

Now, for ⊕: well, we don’t actually need to do anything. This eq term is actually ⊕ itself:

oplus := λp.λq.if p q (¬ q)

In other words, the exclusive disjunction operation acts like an equality check in Boolean logic.

questions.q: Implement a function that returns the length of a list.
questions.a:
Pseudocode:

length(L) :

if L == [] : return 0

if L == (h, t) : return (1 + length(t))

And in OCaml:

let rec length lst =
    match lst with
    | [] -> 0
    | h :: t -> 1 + length t

The logic is very similar to addlist, except that we add 1 instead of the head element.

questions.q: Implement a function that returns the last two elements of a list. The fucntion returns None if it can’t return a value.
questions.a:
lasttwo(L) :

if L == [] : return None

if L == [e] : return None

if L == [e1, e2] : return(e1, e2)

if L == (h, t) : return (lasttwo(t))

let rec lasttwo lst =
  match lst with
  | [] -> None
  | [x] -> None
  | [x;y] -> Some (x,y)
  | h :: t -> lasttwo t;;

questions.q: Implement a function that returns the nth element of a list (indexing). It returns None for an empty list. Hint: use a if then else as the expression for non-empty list case.
questions.a:
at(n, L) :

if L == [] : return None

if L == (h, t) : if (n == 0)return h else at(n − 1, t)

let rec at n lst =
    match lst with
    | [] -> None
    | h :: t -> if n = 0 then Some h else at (n - 1) t;;

questions.label: Part 2 (d)
questions.q: (Advanced) Implement a function that reverses a list. Hint: use an auxiliary function that manipulates two lists.
questions.a:
revaux(newtail, L) :

if L == [] : return newtail

if L == (h, t) : return revaux((h, newtail), t)

rev(L) : revaux([], L)

let rec revaux newtail lst =
    match lst with
    | [] -> newtail
    | h :: t -> revaux (h :: newtail) t
let rev lst = revaux [] lst

This is a non-trivial one. The key here is to start with the logic and a few examples. We know that for lists with zero or one element, we can just return the list itself. What about a list with two elements, like [4, 7]?

• We know that h = 4 and t = [7].

• Our new list should have 4 as the last element. This can be represented as the pair (4, []).

• So our first step should be to create this list, as (h, []).

• Then, when recursing with the tail, we want to do a similar thing with 7 as its new head.

• However, our result now should not be (7, []), but (7, (4, [])).

• This means we need another argument to the recursive function: the tail of the newly created return list. For our first call, this should be [], but after that, it should be the new return list, recursively.

• This is where we need an auxiliary function. While our main function just takes one list as the argument, the auxiliary function will take two lists. Then we just start the computation by calling the auxiliary function, using [] as the first “new” tail.

questions.label: Part 3 (b)
questions.q:
The Fibonacci numbers are defined as follows. Define Fibn as the nth Fibonacci number. Then:

Fib0 = 0

Fib1 = 1

Fibn = Fibn−1 + Fibn−2

Define a term that returns the nth Fibonacci number. Start by “pretending” recursion is allowed in Lambda and define what this “pseudo-term” would look like.
questions.a:
For simplicity, let’s define these additional terms:

is − one := λn. ∧ (¬(is − zero n))(is − zero (pred n))

pred2 := λn.pred (pred n)

We start with the pseudo-term definition:

fib := λn.if (is − zero n)(0)(if (is − one n)(1)(add(fib(predn))(fib(pred2 n))))

Now we “extract” the recursive call and define F:

fib := (λf.λn.if (is − zero n)(0)(if (is − one n)(1)(add(f(predn))(f(pred2 n))))) fib

F := (λf.λn.if (is − zero n)(0)(if (is − one n)(1)(add(f(predn))(f(pred2 n)))))

fib := F fib

We can now use the fixed point operator, since fib is a fixed point of F:

fib := F fib

fib := F Θ F

fib := Θ F

As we can see, we end up with the same result as fact, just with a different F term. To implement other recursive functions, the bulk of the work is in defining F, the rest is simply an application of the fixed point operator.

The \(LABUBU_{TM}\) problem is defined as follows:

\(LABUBU_{TM} = \{\langle M \rangle | labubu \in L(M) \}\)

Prove this problem is undecidable by reduction from the TM Acceptance problem.
questions.a:
Unofficial answer. Canvas has no official solution for this question, so Claude wrote this one. Check it against the lecture material.

Claim: \(LABUBU_{TM}\) is undecidable. Reduce \(A_{TM} = \{\langle M, w\rangle \mid M \text{ accepts } w\}\) to it.

Suppose a TM \(D\) decides \(LABUBU_{TM}\). Build a TM \(H\) that, on input \(\langle M, w\rangle\):

  1. Constructs a new machine \(M'\) that, on input \(x\):
    • if \(x \ne labubu\), rejects;
    • if \(x = labubu\), erases the tape, writes \(w\), runs \(M\) on \(w\), and accepts if \(M\) accepts.
  2. Runs \(D\) on \(\langle M'\rangle\) and returns its answer.

Building \(M'\) only writes down a description; it never runs \(M\), so step 1 always halts.

  • If \(M\) accepts \(w\): \(M'\) accepts \(labubu\), so \(labubu \in L(M')\); \(D\) accepts, so \(H\) accepts.
  • If \(M\) does not accept \(w\) (rejects or loops): \(M'\) never accepts \(labubu\), so \(labubu \notin L(M')\); \(D\) rejects, so \(H\) rejects.

So \(H\) decides \(A_{TM}\), which is undecidable: a contradiction. Hence \(D\) cannot exist and \(LABUBU_{TM}\) is undecidable.
